concept.name: Black-76 model
concept.definition: The Black-76 model is Fischer Black's 1976 adaptation of the Black-Scholes framework to options on forwards and futures: it prices a European option off the forward/futures price directly, discounting the expected payoff at the risk-free rate. It remains the standard quoting convention for options on commodity futures, bond options, caps/floors, and swaptions.
concept.intuition: For an option on a future, you don't need to model spot, storage, and carry separately — the futures price already bundles them, so you just plug the futures price into a Black-Scholes-like formula.
concept.mechanics: Call price = e^(-rT) * [F*N(d1) - K*N(d2)] with d1 = [ln(F/K) + sigma^2*T/2]/(sigma*sqrt(T)); the risk-neutral futures price is driftless (a martingale), which is why no cost-of-carry term appears. Markets routinely invert the formula to quote 'Black implied volatilities' across strikes and maturities.
concept.formula: C = e^(-rT)[F*N(d1) - K*N(d2)]; P = e^(-rT)[K*N(-d2) - F*N(-d1)]; d1 = [ln(F/K) + (sigma^2/2)T]/(sigma*sqrt(T)); d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T).
concept.failure_modes: The lognormal forward assumption fails in the same ways as Black-Scholes (smiles/skews across strikes) and additionally breaks when forwards or rates can go negative — the post-2008 rate environment forced shifted-lognormal and Bachelier (normal) model conventions in rates markets.
concept.misconceptions: Black-76 is not a different theory from Black-Scholes — substituting F = S*e^((r-q)T) recovers the dividend-adjusted Black-Scholes formula, so it is best understood as the same machinery reparameterized to the forward.
concept.example: An at-the-money option on a futures contract at F = 4,000, K = 4,000, T = 0.25, r = 5%, sigma = 15%: d1 = 0.0375, d2 = -0.0375, giving C = e^(-0.0125)*4000*(2*N(0.0375) - 1) ≈ $119.

citations.source: Black, F. (1976), The Pricing of Commodity Contracts, Journal of Financial Economics 3(1-2):167-179 — Crossref record
